The compressor was designed under a NASA Research Announcement (NRA) contract with 2/3 funding from NASA and 1/3 from UTRC.
The design activity was focused on meeting the goal of increasing efficiency at higher work factor while reducing the maximum diameter of the stage.
The impeller tip diameter, impeller rotational speed, and impeller inlet hub and shroud radii were fixed by UTRC to fit within the existing test facility.
The compressor stage featured a 30-degree backsweep impeller design.
The diffuser design included splitter vanes and vane thickening to try to optimize the impeller/diffuser interactions.
The measured polytropic efficiency of 85.5% and stall margin of 7.5% were lower than the pre-test CFD predictions by 2.4 percentage points and 4.5 percentage points, respectively.

Post-test CFD analysis indicated that the performance loss was likely due to unfavorable unsteady impeller/diffuser interactions, impeller/diffuser flow rate mismatch, and flow separation in the radial-to-axial bend.

Recommendations included testing the impeller with a vaneless diffuser, redesigning the diffuser to eliminate the impeller/diffuser mismatch and optimize the vane geometry, and redesigning the radial-to-axial bend to minimize flow separation.
The study highlighted the importance of using unsteady CFD simulations and the need for longer integration times compared to current industry practice.
Inconsistencies in the implementation of a widely used two-equation turbulence model were identified and corrections were recommended.
The compressor achieved a pressure ratio of 4.68 and a work factor of 0.81 at the design exit corrected flow rate of 3 lbm/s.
The compressor was successfully fabricated and tested at NASA Glenn Research Center with no mechanical problems and the running clearances were achieved without impeller rubs.
The design activity was part of the Rotary Wing Project within the NASA Fundamental Aeronautics Program.
The compressor was designed to be representative of the rear stage of an axial-centrifugal aero-engine.
The test instrumentation included steady-state and high-response pressure measurements to provide detailed aerodynamic performance and research quality data.
